program.how: written for ounce-core from the algorithm in the paper or standard; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: MD5 of the 7 strings in the RFC 1321 test suite gives the 7 published 128-bit digests

expected_values_source.what: the 7 digests of the test suite in RFC 1321 section A.5, and the 64 constants T[i] of the RFC's appendix (checked on the host to equal the integer part of 2^32*abs(sin(i)) that the RFC defines)
expected_values_source.note: the digests and constants are data, copied as numbers; the RFC's reference code was not copied

negative_control: built with -DMD5_ROUNDS=3 (the fourth round dropped), 0 of 7 digests match and the program exits 1
not_checked: security claims: MD5 is broken (collisions are practical); this only shows the algorithm as published gives the published digests
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about the authors' hardware)
inputs other than those listed in the RFC test suite (no multi-block streaming or long-message tests)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces exactly the 7 MD5 digests published in RFC 1321. It does not show MD5 is secure (it is not).
